blocks.content: A database has made a promise the moment it tells a client "your write succeeded": that data will still be there after a crash, a power outage, or a process getting killed mid-operation. Keeping that promise while also being fast is a genuinely hard problem, and the mechanism nearly every serious database relies on to solve it is the Write-Ahead Log, or WAL: never change the real data until the intent to change it has already been safely written down first.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396522578-351072524.png
blocks.alt: A change that only ever existed in memory disappears completely the moment a crash happens, unless something durable recorded it first

blocks.content: 1. The Problem: Durability Without Sacrificing Speed
blocks.text: 1. The Problem: Durability Without Sacrificing Speed

blocks.content: The straightforward way to guarantee durability would be to write every single change directly to its final location on disk, immediately, before ever acknowledging success to the client. The problem is that updating data in its final location, an index page in a B+ Tree, a row in a table file, is a slow, random-access operation, exactly the kind of expensive disk seek covered under B-Trees and B+ Trees elsewhere in this section.

A WAL resolves this tension directly: instead of making the slow, final update durable immediately, it makes a small, fast, sequential note of the intended change durable first, and applies the actual, slower update to the real data structure afterward, on its own schedule.

It helps to picture the alternative directly to see why this matters. Without a WAL, every single write would need to update its final location on disk, synchronously, before acknowledging success, an index page here, a data row there, each one a separate, expensive random-access operation happening on the critical path of every single write a client makes.

It is worth naming plainly why this specific design was such a breakthrough historically, it lets a database offer the exact same durability guarantee as writing everything synchronously to its final location, while paying only the cost of a cheap, sequential append on the hot path, deferring the more expensive real update to whenever the system has spare capacity to do it.

This same tension, wanting both speed and safety without giving up either, shows up constantly across system design, and the write-ahead log is one of the cleanest, most enduring examples of resolving it elegantly rather than simply picking one side of the trade-off and accepting the other cost.
2. How It Works: Log First, Then Apply
blocks.text: 2. How It Works: Log First, Then Apply

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785283872895-686869327.png
blocks.alt: Every change is written to the log before it is applied to the real, underlying data structure

blocks.content: Before any change touches the actual table or index, it is first appended as an entry to the write-ahead log: what changed, and what the new value is (or enough information to redo or undo the change). Only once that log entry is safely on disk does the database consider the write durable, and only after that does it go on to actually apply the change to the real data, whenever it is convenient to do so.

# simplified WAL write path
def write(key, value):
    wal.append(f"SET {key} = {value}")  # durable, sequential
    wal.fsync()                          # force it to actual disk
    acknowledge_client()                 # now safe to tell the caller "done"
    apply_to_memtable(key, value)        # the slower, real update can happen after

blocks.content: 2.1 Redo and undo information
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785283875028-240565810.png
blocks.alt: A log entry can carry redo information, to reapply a committed change, or undo information, to reverse one that never fully committed

blocks.content: A log entry typically carries enough information to redo the change (reapply it, useful for recovering committed writes) and sometimes also enough to undo it (reverse it, useful if a transaction was in progress but never actually committed before the crash). Which of these a specific database implementation emphasizes depends on its exact recovery algorithm, but the core idea, logging enough information to reconstruct the correct final state, stays the same either way.

This ordering, log then apply, is non-negotiable for the guarantee to hold. If the real data were updated first and the log written second, a crash landing exactly between those two steps would leave a change applied to the real data with no record of it ever having happened, defeating the entire purpose the log exists for in the first place.

Some systems, PostgreSQL among them, lean primarily on redo-oriented logging combined with a separate mechanism for handling uncommitted transactions, while others implement full undo logging directly, the exact split varies by database, but the underlying goal, being able to reconstruct a fully correct final state after any possible crash point, remains identical across all of them.
3. Why Sequential Writes Are So Much Faster
blocks.text: 3. Why Sequential Writes Are So Much Faster

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785283876979-570286156.png
blocks.alt: A log is only ever appended to, never modified in place, which makes every single write to it sequential and fast

blocks.content: A write-ahead log is, by design, an append-only file, new entries are always added to the end, and existing entries are never modified or reordered. This is exactly the same sequential-write advantage covered under LSM Trees elsewhere in this section, sequential disk writes are dramatically cheaper than random ones, which is precisely why logging the intent first, sequentially, and applying the real, potentially random-access change second, is faster overall than trying to make every real update durable immediately.

This also means the log itself needs a mechanism to know where it left off after a crash, a common technique is including a checksum or sequence number with each entry, so recovery can reliably detect and stop at the exact point where the log was mid-write when the crash occurred, rather than accidentally replaying a corrupted, half-written final entry.

It is a useful, if slightly imprecise, comparison to think of the write-ahead log as behaving like the LSM Tree memtable-and-flush pattern in miniature, both convert what would otherwise be scattered, random writes into a single, fast, sequential stream, and defer the more expensive organizational work to happen later, out of the critical path.

This is also why a write-ahead log is often placed on its own dedicated, fast storage device separate from the main data files in performance-sensitive deployments, isolating its purely sequential write pattern from the more random access patterns the rest of the database generates against its data files.
4. Recovery After a Crash: Replaying the Log
blocks.text: 4. Recovery After a Crash: Replaying the Log

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785283878932-445043429.png
blocks.alt: On restart after a crash, the database reads the log and replays every entry to fully reconstruct its state

blocks.content: This is where the entire design pays off. If the database crashes at any point, even mid-write, recovery is straightforward: read the write-ahead log from the last known consistent point, and replay every logged entry in order, reapplying each change exactly as it was originally intended. By the time replay finishes, the database is back to exactly the state it was in the instant before the crash, with nothing lost, because every acknowledged write was already safely recorded in the log before the crash ever happened.

It is worth noting recovery time is directly proportional to how much log needs replaying, which is precisely the quantity checkpointing exists to bound, a database with no checkpointing at all could, in the extreme, need to replay its entire history since the beginning of time after a crash, an unacceptable outcome checkpointing is specifically designed to prevent.
4.1 Why replay is deterministic and safe
blocks.text: 4.1 Why replay is deterministic and safe

blocks.content: A crucial property that makes this recovery process trustworthy: replaying the exact same sequence of logged changes always produces the exact same final state, no matter how many times it is replayed or how the crash happened to interrupt the original work. This determinism is what lets a database recover confidently and automatically, without needing a human to inspect and manually reconcile anything after an unexpected crash.

This same determinism property is also what makes it safe to replay a write-ahead log onto a replica that is running on entirely different hardware than the original primary, since the guarantee is about the logical sequence of changes, not anything tied to the specific machine that originally produced them.
5. Checkpointing: Keeping the Log From Growing Forever
blocks.text: 5. Checkpointing: Keeping the Log From Growing Forever

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396522580-397926942.png
blocks.alt: A checkpoint confirms recent changes are safely reflected in the real data files, letting old log entries finally be discarded

blocks.content: Left unchecked, a write-ahead log would grow forever, every single change ever made, kept indefinitely. A checkpoint solves this: periodically, the database confirms that all changes up to a certain point in the log have been fully and safely applied to the real, underlying data files, and once confirmed, everything in the log before that point becomes unnecessary and can be safely discarded.

This is a direct trade-off in itself, checkpointing too rarely means an unnecessarily large log and a longer replay time after a crash, while checkpointing too aggressively spends more resources doing the actual, slower data writes checkpointing requires.

Checkpoint frequency is a tunable configuration in essentially every real database, and it directly trades two costs against each other, more frequent checkpoints mean faster recovery after a crash but more ongoing background write overhead during normal operation, less frequent checkpoints mean the opposite, cheaper normal operation but a longer replay if a crash actually happens.

A useful mental model for a checkpoint is a save point in a long process, everything before it is confirmed, safe, and no longer needs to be replayed, everything after it is what recovery would actually need to redo, which is exactly why a more recent checkpoint means a faster recovery the next time it is actually needed.
6. WAL and the ACID "D": Durability
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785283882616-622343159.png
blocks.alt: The Durability guarantee in ACID is, in most real databases, implemented specifically through a write-ahead log

blocks.content: If you have encountered the ACID properties, Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability, elsewhere, it is worth connecting them directly to this mechanism: Durability, the promise that a committed transaction survives a crash, is in practice implemented by exactly this write-ahead logging technique in the overwhelming majority of real relational databases.

It is worth being precise that Durability is specifically about surviving a crash after a transaction has been confirmed as committed, it says nothing about the other three ACID letters, Atomicity, Consistency, and Isolation are separate guarantees handled by other mechanisms entirely, even though a WAL sometimes plays a supporting role in Atomicity too, by recording enough information to fully undo a transaction that never completed.
6.1 A quick way to remember the connection
blocks.text: 6.1 A quick way to remember the connection

blocks.content: A simple way to hold onto this: Atomicity and Isolation are mostly about correctness during normal operation, Consistency is about the data always satisfying its own rules, and Durability is specifically the one guarantee that has to survive a crash, which is exactly the single narrow problem a write-ahead log is built to solve.

This framing also helps explain why Durability is so often discussed separately from the other three ACID letters in practice, Atomicity, Consistency, and Isolation are largely enforced through locking, versioning, and transaction management logic running during normal operation, while Durability specifically has to reason about the one moment none of that logic can help, a machine failing entirely and unexpectedly.
7. WAL in LSM Trees vs B-Tree Databases
blocks.text: 7. WAL in LSM Trees vs B-Tree Databases

blocks.content: The exact same mechanism protects two very differently shaped storage engines. In an LSM Tree, covered fully elsewhere in this section, the WAL protects the in-memory memtable, which would otherwise be entirely lost on a crash before its next flush to disk. In a traditional B+ Tree database, the WAL protects any change that has been acknowledged to a client but not yet physically written into its final page location on disk. Different storage engine, same fundamental durability problem, same fundamental fix.

This shared reliance on the exact same durability mechanism, despite the two storage engines otherwise looking quite different, is a good example of a broader pattern in system design, very different systems often converge on the same underlying primitive to solve the same underlying problem, and recognizing that shared primitive is often more valuable than memorizing each system as an unrelated special case.

It is a useful exercise, when learning either storage engine, to explicitly ask what exactly the write-ahead log is protecting in that specific context, the memtable in one case, an in-progress page update in the other, since naming that specific, concrete thing being protected tends to make the whole mechanism click far more solidly than treating it as an abstract, generic durability layer.
8. Group Commit: Batching for Performance
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785283885195-92385610.png
blocks.alt: Multiple separate writes get batched into a single log flush, cutting down dramatically on the number of expensive fsync calls needed

blocks.content: Making a write truly durable requires an fsync, a call that forces the operating system to actually flush data to physical disk, rather than leaving it sitting in a buffer that a power loss could still wipe out. fsync calls are relatively expensive, so most databases use group commit: batching several separate, concurrent writes together and performing just one fsync for the whole batch, rather than one fsync per individual write.

This trades a tiny amount of added latency (waiting a few milliseconds to see if other writes will join the same batch) for a large improvement in overall throughput, since the expensive part, the fsync itself, now gets shared across many writes instead of paid for individually by each one.

The batching window is itself tunable, a slightly longer window collects more writes into each fsync, improving throughput further under heavy concurrent load, at the cost of very slightly higher latency for any single individual write waiting for its batch to close.
8.1 What fsync actually guarantees
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396522580-636157229.png
blocks.alt: A write sitting only in an OS buffer is still at risk from a power loss; fsync is what forces it onto physical disk for real

blocks.content: It is worth being precise about what "written to disk" actually means here. A normal file write often lands first in an operating system buffer in memory, not physical storage, and a sudden power loss can still lose it from there. fsync is the specific system call that forces the operating system to flush that buffer all the way to physical storage, and only after fsync returns successfully can a write genuinely be considered crash-safe.

It is worth knowing this has a real, measurable cost, an fsync call can take anywhere from under a millisecond on fast, modern storage to several milliseconds on slower disks, which is precisely the cost group commit exists to amortize across many writes at once rather than paying in full for every single one individually.
9. Real-World Usage

{"headers":["System","How it uses a WAL"],"rows":[["PostgreSQL","Has a WAL subsystem as a core, foundational part of its architecture, also reused for replication"],["MySQL (InnoDB)","Uses a redo log serving the exact same write-ahead purpose"],["Kafka","Its entire storage model is essentially an append-only log, the same core idea applied as the primary data model, not just a durability mechanism"]]}

Kafka in particular is worth pausing on, since it takes this idea to its logical conclusion, rather than treating the log purely as an internal recovery mechanism hidden from users, Kafka exposes the append-only log itself as the primary, user-facing data model, an entire class of systems now builds directly on top of that same core write-ahead-log idea as a first-class abstraction.

MySQL innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit setting is a concrete, well-known example of this exact durability-versus-performance trade-off exposed directly as a configuration knob, letting an operator explicitly choose how strictly every commit waits on a real fsync versus batching for higher throughput.
9.1 A second job for the WAL: replication
blocks.text: 9.1 A second job for the WAL: replication

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785283889510-12912632.png
blocks.alt: The same log a database uses for crash recovery can also be streamed to replicas, which replay it to stay continuously in sync

blocks.content: The write-ahead log turns out to be useful for more than crash recovery alone. Since it already contains a complete, ordered record of every change made, many databases stream that same log to replica servers, which replay it continuously to stay in sync with the primary, exactly the mechanism behind PostgreSQL streaming replication. This is a clean example of a mechanism built for one purpose, durability, turning out to elegantly solve a second problem, replication, almost for free.

This dual purpose is not a coincidence either, both crash recovery and replication ultimately need the exact same thing, a reliable, ordered record of every change that happened, which is exactly what a write-ahead log already provides for free once it exists for durability in the first place.
10. Common Mistakes

["Assuming a write is durable the moment it is accepted in memory, without confirming it, and specifically the WAL entry behind it, has actually been fsynced to disk.","Disabling or weakening fsync behavior purely for a performance benchmark, without understanding that doing so directly trades away real crash durability.","Forgetting that checkpointing has its own real cost, and tuning it purely to minimize log size without considering recovery time after a crash."]
items: Assuming a write is durable the moment it is accepted in memory, without confirming it, and specifically the WAL entry behind it, has actually been fsynced to disk.
Disabling or weakening fsync behavior purely for a performance benchmark, without understanding that doing so directly trades away real crash durability.
Forgetting that checkpointing has its own real cost, and tuning it purely to minimize log size without considering recovery time after a crash.

blocks.content: ["Storing the WAL on the same physical disk as the primary data files without considering that a single disk failure could then take down both the data and the means of recovering it.","Ignoring WAL disk usage growth in monitoring, only to discover during an incident that checkpointing had silently stopped keeping up."]
items: Storing the WAL on the same physical disk as the primary data files without considering that a single disk failure could then take down both the data and the means of recovering it.
Ignoring WAL disk usage growth in monitoring, only to discover during an incident that checkpointing had silently stopped keeping up.

blocks.content: A further, easy-to-overlook mistake is running with fsync effectively disabled in a test or staging environment for speed, and never re-verifying that production actually has it correctly enabled, a gap that only becomes visible the hard way, during a real crash that loses data everyone assumed was safe.

It is also worth double checking, for any managed or cloud-hosted database, exactly what durability guarantee the default configuration actually provides, since defaults optimized for benchmark-friendly throughput numbers do not always match what a given application actually needs to promise its own users.
11. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This
blocks.text: 11. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This

blocks.content: Strong answers explain why logging first is actually faster overall, not just safer, sequential appends versus random final writes, rather than presenting the WAL as purely a safety mechanism with a performance cost. Being able to connect it directly to the ACID durability guarantee, and to name how it protects both LSM Tree memtables and B+ Tree pages, shows this is understood as a general pattern, not a feature specific to one particular database.
A write-ahead log turns "did this survive a crash" from a question answered by hope into one answered by a simple, mechanical replay.

A good follow-up to anticipate is being asked to compare the durability guarantee here against an in-memory-only cache that accepts data loss on a crash, articulating clearly that a WAL is specifically what a system reaches for the moment losing acknowledged data becomes unacceptable, versus a cache where an occasional loss is a tolerable, even expected, trade-off, shows the guarantee is understood as a deliberate choice, not a default every system needs.

It is also worth being ready to explain, briefly, why this problem cannot simply be solved by writing to faster storage instead, faster disks reduce the cost difference between sequential and random writes somewhat, but they do not eliminate the fundamental risk of a crash happening between an in-memory change and its eventual durable write, which is the actual problem a write-ahead log solves, independent of how fast the underlying storage happens to be.
Key Takeaways

["A Write-Ahead Log records the intent to change data, durably and sequentially, before that change is actually applied to its final location.","This makes writes fast (sequential appends) while still guaranteeing durability, resolving a real tension between speed and safety.","Recovery after a crash simply replays the log from the last checkpoint, reconstructing exactly the state that existed right before the crash.","Checkpointing periodically confirms recent changes are safely persisted, allowing old log entries to be discarded before the log grows without bound.","The WAL is the practical mechanism behind the \"Durability\" guarantee in ACID, and it protects both LSM Tree memtables and traditional B+ Tree pages the same way.","Group commit batches multiple writes into a single expensive fsync call, trading a small amount of latency for significantly higher throughput."]
items: A Write-Ahead Log records the intent to change data, durably and sequentially, before that change is actually applied to its final location.
This makes writes fast (sequential appends) while still guaranteeing durability, resolving a real tension between speed and safety.
Recovery after a crash simply replays the log from the last checkpoint, reconstructing exactly the state that existed right before the crash.
Checkpointing periodically confirms recent changes are safely persisted, allowing old log entries to be discarded before the log grows without bound.
The WAL is the practical mechanism behind the "Durability" guarantee in ACID, and it protects both LSM Tree memtables and traditional B+ Tree pages the same way.
Group commit batches multiple writes into a single expensive fsync call, trading a small amount of latency for significantly higher throughput.

blocks.content: Read this topic alongside LSM Trees and B-Trees and B+ Trees in this same section, together they show how a single, simple idea, log first, apply second, underpins durability for two storage engines that otherwise look almost nothing alike on the surface.

Once this pattern clicks, it becomes visible almost everywhere durability actually matters, not just inside a single database, distributed consensus protocols, message queues, and even version control systems all lean on some flavor of the same idea, record the intent durably and in order first, then let the more complex, final state catch up afterward.
